title: Supplement use is a mass consumer-health practice shaped by age, income, identity, and perceived personal importance
source_unit: Pew Research Center, About 8 in 10 Americans take supplements, and many see them as important to their health, September 2026
geography: United States; adults nationally with age, gender, race/ethnicity, education, and income comparisons

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew American Trends Panel survey

any_supplement.unit: percent currently taking at least one supplement for health

vitamins_or_minerals.unit: percent currently taking vitamins or minerals

omega_oils.unit: percent currently taking omega oil supplements

observations.method: Pew Research Center survey of 3,554 U.S. adults in the American Trends Panel, fielded July 6-12, 2026; respondents were given a definition including vitamins, minerals, herbals, protein powders, melatonin, and probiotics, excluding prescription and over-the-counter drugs.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported product-use measures and do not establish medical need, product quality, health benefit, safety, spending, adherence, or whether use substitutes for clinical care.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults nationally, with type-specific and demographic comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: High supplement use may represent prevention, treatment of a diagnosed deficiency, routine, cultural practice, fitness goals, influencer exposure, or consumer experimentation; the aggregate does not imply a common motivation.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Pew survey; age-group comparisons use weighted subgroup universes

any_supplement_age_65_plus.unit: percent of adults age 65 and older

vitamins_under_30.unit: percent of adults ages 18-29 taking vitamins or minerals

vitamins_age_65_plus.unit: percent of adults age 65 and older taking vitamins or minerals

protein_under_30.unit: percent of adults ages 18-29 taking protein supplements

protein_age_65_plus.unit: percent of adults age 65 and older taking protein supplements

observations.method: Pew age-group comparison of reported supplement use by product type.
observations.uncertainty: Age differences are descriptive and do not identify health status, fitness behavior, marketing exposure, income, or clinical advice; product categories overlap.
observations.counterinterpretation: Older adults may use vitamins in response to age-related nutritional needs while younger adults may use protein products for fitness or identity reasons; the survey cannot distinguish these pathways.

observations.period: July 2026; perceived importance among supplement users

denominator.unit: U.S. adults taking each supplement category; category-specific denominators

vitamins_extremely_very_important.unit: percent of vitamin/mineral users saying supplements are extremely or very important to their health

vitamins_somewhat_important.unit: percent of vitamin/mineral users saying somewhat important

observations.method: Conditional Pew estimates among users of each supplement type; importance is a perception measure, not a clinical efficacy measure.
observations.uncertainty: Importance judgments can reflect belief, routine, symptom interpretation, marketing, clinician advice, or perceived identity; they do not establish benefit or causality.
observations.subgroup: Users of vitamins/minerals, protein, omega oils, herbals, and other supplements.
observations.counterinterpretation: A product can be considered important without being medically effective, and reported importance can coexist with uncertainty about ingredients, regulation, interactions, and appropriate dose.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Pew survey; weighted subgroup comparisons

asian_omega_oils.unit: percent of Asian adults; estimate representative of English speakers where applicable

postgraduate_any_supplement.unit: percent of adults with postgraduate education

observations.method: Pew weighted subgroup table using gender, race/ethnicity, education, and adjusted family-income tiers.
observations.uncertainty: Subgroup differences are descriptive and may reflect age, health, income, education, access, cultural practice, or product marketing; they do not establish unequal medical need or effect.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults by gender, race/ethnicity, education, and adjusted family income.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher use among wealthier and more educated adults may reflect purchasing power and health optimization, while lower use may reflect cost or different care routes; use rates alone cannot determine welfare or adequacy.

boundary: This record adds a consumer-health and belief layer: supplements are a mass household practice whose product mix and perceived importance vary by age, income, gender, identity, and likely wellness culture. It does not establish efficacy, safety, clinical need, spending, substitution for care, or causal health outcomes.
